profile.campus: Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia (Equinix Ashburn campus, Data Center Alley)
profile.reading:
This building operates as Equinix's DC3 data center at 44470 Chilum Place in Ashburn, Virginia, one node in Equinix's cluster of buildings spread across Loudoun County's Data Center Alley, set apart from Equinix's Filigree Court cluster nearby on a separate street within the same campus area. Equinix's own DC3 facility page publishes concrete numbers rather than general marketing text, 67,038 square feet of space, N+2 power redundancy on both UPS and generator systems, generator autonomy rated for 30 hours or more at full load, N+2 cooling redundancy, a one story reinforced concrete building with a raised floor rated at 200 psf and slab rated at 3,000 psf, and nine compliance certifications, HECVAT, HIPAA, ISO 9001, ISO 22301, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53/FISMA High, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, and SOC 2 Type II. Equinix does not publish an IT load or utility power figure in megawatts for DC3 itself, so this entry does not assign one.

Ashburn's status as the center of Data Center Alley predates Equinix's arrival. AOL built what is generally regarded as the area's first data center, its Dulles Technology Center, in 1997 to support its dial up internet subscriber base, and the fiber capacity that project pulled into Loudoun County helped seed the cluster of interconnected facilities that followed. Equinix opened its own first Ashburn building, DC1, in the late 1990s, and its second building, DC2, earned a reputation, per Data Center Dynamics, as one of the most connected buildings on earth. Loudoun County's data center corridor has since grown into what Data Center Dynamics describes as roughly 10 million square feet of built space consuming on the order of 1 gigawatt of electrical power region wide, a figure covering every operator in the corridor rather than Equinix alone.

Equinix's own Washington D.C. metro listing page currently names and links 15 facilities together, DC1 through DC6, DC10 through DC16, DC21, and DC22, with most addresses in Ashburn and at least one, DC14, in nearby Manassas. Equinix does not publish a combined power or square footage total for that group of buildings, and Equinix markets DC1 through DC6 and DC10 through DC12 collectively as offering access to one of the top three internet peering exchange markets on the East Coast, without singling out DC3's own peering density or customer roster.

Every data center on this campus now also sits inside Virginia's evolving electricity regulatory framework for large power users. The State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates in November 2026 that raise a typical residential bill by about 16 dollars a month, while creating a new GS-5 rate class specifically for data centers, effective January 1, 2027, that requires large demand customers like Equinix's Ashburn buildings to sign 14 year minimum contracts with cost coverage guarantees, according to Inside Climate News's reporting on the commission's decision.

reading.body:
Equinix DC3 is a 67,038-square-foot facility in Ashburn, Virginia, part of Equinix's multi-building Ashburn campus in Data Center Alley, Loudoun County. The operator publishes no power capacity figure for DC3 itself, only that the campus offers N+2 power and cooling redundancy with 30+ hours of generator autonomy at full load. Equinix's DC2 building on the same campus, described as representative of general campus specifications, operates at a minimum cabinet density of 4kVA and holds certifications including ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, and NIST 800-53/FISMA High, though these certifications are not confirmed for DC3 specifically by published sources.

Data Center Alley, anchored by AOL's 1997 Dulles Technology Center and Equinix's late-1990s DC1 and DC2, is described as the greatest concentration of data center space on the planet at roughly 10 million square feet. Equinix's Ashburn campus serves one of the top three internet peering exchange markets on the US East Coast and has expanded well beyond its initial two buildings into numbered facilities reaching at least the twenties. In Virginia overall, 330 data center facilities are mapped in open sources, but only 23 publish power capacity figures; those 23 facilities total 1,375 megawatts, and this campus ranks 24th by published megawattage in the state, meaning no published figure places it within the top disclosed capacity sites.

The absence of DC3's own published power or square footage means its significance to AI scaling cannot be read from operator specifications. Whether this facility contributes materially to grid-constrained AI compute depends on undisclosed capacity details and current tenant workloads, neither available in public sources. The Ashburn campus as a whole remains foundational to US internet infrastructure and peering, but for this specific building's role in AI deployment, the published record contains no basis for assessment.
